detailedDesc:
Water Goal 1

Step 1 is to drink 1 liter of water per day. You are welcome to drink more than 1 liter of water, but never less. This step is a minimum not a maximum. To facilitate water tracking, you can find a 1 liter bottle in just about any store. Nalgene bottles, steel water containers, and protein blender bottles are all available in 1 liter sizes.

Water and water alone counts towards your water goal. If you add lemon or lime juice, that water does not count toward the goal. Once you consume 1 liter of plain water, you are welcome to add freshly squeezed lemon or lime juice (do not buy lime/lemon juice) into water.

Drinking water is the first step because of its importance to our performance. Next to oxygen, water is the most important substance in the human body. It is used in every metabolic process (digestion, assimilation, elimination, respiration, and maintaining body temperature). If you are not drinking enough water, you are inhibiting nutrient and oxygen delivery to your brain and muscles, and you are slowing down your metabolic fat burning process.

Your body is 50-60% water overall. Fat tissue is 20% water, and muscle, brains, and blood are all about 80% water. This means hydration levels affect both your mental and physical performance as well as your overall heath.

Dehydration is defined as a loss of water equal to 1% + of bodyweight. If you are 150 pounds that is only 23 ounces, so if you are not actively drinking water throughout the day, you are dehydrated. Thirst is most commonly perceived between 1-2% bodyweight loss in water, but your metabolic process start suffering long before that (at about .5% bodyweight loss). Because we can become dehydrated so easily, don't wait to get thirsty to drink water. Get ahead-drink early and often.

Ideally your water consumption should be spread out throughout the day. For example, if you drink 1 liter of water by 10am, I would recommend still taking in fluids throughout the rest of the day. For example, you could have a glass of green tea with lunch and sparkling water with lime with dinner.

You are not just what you eat; you are also what you drink...or don't drink!

Stay ahead of the curve and drink water throughout the day. Your objective for step 1 is to drink 1 liter of water per day. More if you like, but never less.

lesson:
How to use this course:


Welcome to Thrive, a truly behavior-based nutrition course, created specifically to promote long-term progress.

We focus on behavior instead of drowning you with facts and figures. Do you know that vegetables are good for you? Of course you do. Are you are eating enough of them?

Odds are you aren't, and that's the type of problem this course will fix. We will require you to eat adequate vegetables at the right time, but we're not going to tell you anything about the suphurphane content in broccoli and how that helps with phase 2 detoxification as a conjugate.

Instead, this course offers what we find lacking in other programs: the practical how-to at a basic level that gets real, obtainable results. Thrive is a program that incorporates accountability, measurable tasks, lifestyle components, and–most importantly–results.

The most basic definition of good nutrition is food that makes the body function better. Food either improves function or it doesn't. Thrive is simple: we build habits using foods that improve function.

Too many changes at once is a recipe for failure, so we take the approach of adding good habits before subtracting suboptimal foods. In fact, this entire level one course improves function without telling you what you can't eat. Establishing a foundation of good nutrition habits is critical for long-term function and performance. Whether the goal is maximizing athletic potential or simply a healthy lifestyle, the Gymnastic Bodies way is one of personal excellence.

Just as an Olympic or professional athlete is built over time, so will your own personal excellence take time to develop.

In this program, you are expected to adhere to all your habits six days a week; Sundays are always off days. If you adhere to your habits for six days in a row, you will get a new task every Monday and Thursday. If you don't complete your tasks for six days in a row, you won't get your next task. I expect results from you, and if I don't get em', you don't get the next step.

At this point, you have one habit to master over the next six days: drink 1L of water per day. You do not have access to the full course because we focus on practical progress, not scratching your intellectual curiosity.

In addition to your first habit, I want you to take some before pictures. The pictures are for you and won't be shared with others. We will take pictures again at the end so you can see your progress.

There are 9 1/2 weeks of material here for you to master. Each step toward your nutritional foundation will take effort. If you don't get it out of the gate just stick with it; quitting is not an option. We build success upon success. We don't compromise in our course and we expect that you won't compromise on your personal goals.

Okay guys, get the water down, upload that before picture, and you're done with step one for today!

In Fats 101 we are going to cover good sources of fat to incorporate into your diet and some to stay away from. We will overview healthy fat sources–oils, nuts and seeds, dairy, fish, and eggs–and unhealthy fats such as trans fats and industrial seed oils. This is going to be all practical; theoretical information will come later. Fats 101 is the nuts and bolts you need to get going right now.

Optimal fat choices

Oils:

The best oils are unrefined and taste like the nut, seed, or fruit (such as olives), from which they were mechanically (expeller) pressed without solvents. They are freshly processed, protectively packaged, and quickly delivered. If the oil don't taste like the nut, seed, or fruit it came from, that means the oil has been refined, bleached, and/or deodorized, resulting in a massive loss of nutrients. Heavily processes oils could also contain trans fats. Here are some great sources of fat from oil to incorporate into your meals:
  • Olive oil got its good name in the ancient Mediterranean because olives could be pressed and preserved easily without high pressure equipment and refrigeration technology that hadn't yet been invented. The ease of pressing oil from olives makes this the number one oil choice for fresh and nutritious oils. Olive oil is high in phyosterols, chlorophyll, magnesium, vitamin E, and carotene. Look for olive oil sold in opaque contains, and check labels for "organic" and "extra virgin." One caution is that you should not to cook with olive oil, because heat of about 300 degrees damages it. Due to this restriction, it is ideal for salad dressings.
  • Coconut oil is better for cooking because it handles 400 degrees. Coconut oil is a good source of medium chain triglycerides (MCTs) and a ready-to-use, convenient source of fuel that doesn't spike blood sugar. Coconut oil is an anti-viral, antibacterial, and anti-fungal to boot. Coconut meat and butter are also good choices (coconut flour and sugar aren't). If you use coconut oil to cook your food and it doesn't add a coconut flavor, odds are it was deodorized, resulting in a loss of Vitamin E, tocotrienols, and carotene. In extreme cases, processing may leave behind some trans fats. Look for organic, extra virgin, and unrefined coconut oil.
  • Other good oils include avocado and macadamia nut, but they are tougher to turn into oils, so they have a higher chance of being refined, bleached, or deodorized. When looking for these two, follow the same standards as olive oil.

Nuts and seeds:

They are a good food, but not a superfood. There are a lot of good nutrients in nuts–but there are some anti-nutrients too. Without the anti-nutrients, nuts would be a superfood. To mitigate anti-nutrients, buy dry roasted nuts or to soak them.
  • Macadamia nuts are low in phytic acid and one of the most nutritious nuts with a decent amount of omega-3 fatty acids. They are a good source of fiber, B vitamins, iron, magnesium, manganese, and antioxidant minerals.
  • Other acceptable nuts include pistachios, cashews, pecans, walnuts, Brazil nuts, hazelnuts, and flax seeds (but the moderate nutritional profile may not be worth suffering the poor flavor of flax seeds!).
Nuts are really convenient to carry around or have available at work for snacks. That said, nuts should not be a staple of your diet. A handful here or there or nut butters are the best way to use them. Nut flours should be avoided altogether. Dairy: Either dairy agrees with you or it doesn't. If it doesn't, then no big deal. If you can eat dairy, it is a delicious way to consume a nutrient-rich fat. Dairy products have long been valued as a nutritional powerhouse. Genghis Khan and his Mongolian warriors practically lived off dairy. The Mongolians used mares for milk and did used two unique methods to consume it:
  • Fermented the milk, making what they called ‘Koumiss'
  • Dried the milk out in the sun, making powdered milk; they would bring this with them on long journeys
Mongolian warriors were definitely on to something. Dairy is the best source of CLA, a type of fat that is toxic to cancer cells and promotes the use of body fat for fuel. The body cannot make CLA, so you must obtain it from foods you eat. Dairy is also high in other essential nutrients like B vitamins and iodine. It is important to make sure you are eating dairy from healthy cows, preferably grass-fed cows. We consume dairy in many forms, each with their own benefits. Assume going forward that I am strictly referring to full fat dairy. If you reduce the fat in dairy, you reduce the CLA as well as any chance of omega-3s.
  • Fermented Dairy Products are full of beneficial bacteria that eat lactose and other milk sugars. These "beneficial bacteria" help maintain the integrity of the gut lining, act as natural antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals, boosting immune function and controlling inflammation in the gut and subsequently the entire body.
  • 90% of Kefir on the market is low fat, which completely defeats the purpose of kefir. If you can't get whole milk/full fat kefir, then just avoid it all together. Also avoid any flavoring additives to kefir.
  • The same applies to Greek yogurt: skip the low-fat and non-fat varieties that dominate the market in favor of whole milk/full fat varieties.
  • Real cheese–such as a wheel of parmesan, not a can of spray cheese–has a number of health benefits. If the label lists "pasteurized process" as an ingredient, it's not a cheese you want. Real cheese and fermented dairy are concentrated versions of milk, high in vitamins and minerals, calcium, zinc, A, D B, and K2 as well as CLA. Good cheese choices are aged Cheddar, Colby, Provolone, Gouda, and blue cheese. The benefits also extend to goat cheeses and sheep milk cheese.
  • Butter–real butter, not margarine or any other fake food–is high in MCT as well as butyric acid, another easily digestible short-chain fatty acid (saturated). It is also rich in fat-soluble vitamins, particularly K2. Butter is great for high heat cooking and flavor. Grass-fed cow's butter is the optimal choice.
  • Ghee/Clarified Butter/Drawn Butter is capable of withstanding very high heats, making it a great option to fry foods with. Ghee is made through a simple process of boiling butter and pouring off the butterfat, leaving behind the proteins and the milk solids.
  • Heavy cream lands somewhere between milk and butter. It is a great choice to add to morning coffee.

Fish:

Fish is primarily a protein, but we are going to talk about fish in Healthy Fats 101 because fish contains both the prize winner and runner up of all fats: DHA and EPA respectively. DHA and EPA have important roles in health. Regular consumption of DHA and EPA rich fats
  • Improve brain development and cognition
  • Reduce inflammation
  • Improve blood pressure and triglyceride levels
  • Keep our arteries and platelets healthy
The best sources of DHA and EPA are cold water fish, including anchovy, mackerel, salmon, sardines, herring, sablefish, roe, and caviar.

Eggs:

We can't talk about fat without mentioning eggs. One egg provides 13 essential nutrients, a majority of which are in the yolk. Eggs are one of the only good sources of Vitamin D in food, and they are rich in B vitamins and choline. Choline in eggs works out particularly well since choline improves cognition, and we typically eat eggs in the morning when we need our brains to wake up. Don't worry about the cholesterol in eggs. When we are concerned about cholesterol, we are actually concerned about the protein carrier molecules HDL ("good cholesterol") and LDL ("bad cholesterol"). Eggs increase HDL, which is the lipoprotein you want higher in ratio to LDL. Besides, eating egg whites is absolutely pointless–if you buy omega-3 enriched eggs (as you should) and ditch the yolk, you ditch the omega-3s along with it. Two things really matter when buying eggs: The listed omega-3 content (above 115mg/egg) and the USDA Certified Organic label. To determine the quality of your eggs beyond these labels, see how orange or yellow the yolk is. Chickens are omnivores despite the "vegetarian" claims on some egg cartons. Chickens pick and scratch at the ground for worms and critters which dramatically increases the nutrients and quality of taste. The more chickens forage for their own food, the more nutritious the egg, and the darker yellow/orange the yolk becomes. Specifically, carotenoids that cause deeper yellow-orange yolk coloring are xanthophylls, which are more readily absorbed in the yolks. Lutein is one kind of xanthophyll, and a lot of lutein means a lot more orange. Orange yolks also mean you are getting higher levels of vitamins A, D, and E; more beta-carotene; and more omega-3s.

Disadvantageous sources of fat

Trans Fat (Hydrogenated): After 1977, food manufacturers were forced to stop using fats like lard, beef tallow, and butter for fried foods. At the time, they thought it was a good idea replace them with partially solid oils. They turned this previously liquid fat into a partial solid by adding hydrogen to various vegetable oils. There are two benefits to this process: 1) It prolongs the shelf life of the oil, and 2) It "improves" the texture (i.e., making margarine spreadable). Notice, the benefits have nothing to do with health. In fact, there hydrogenated fats present notable health concerns:
  • Trans fats inhibit DHA's myelin-building process in the brain
  • Trans fats create inflammation in the brain, significantly increasing odds of a stroke
What's more troubling is that is food labels can list 0 grams of trans fats so long as the food contains less than .5 a gram of trans fat per serving. Two grams a day (4 servings) is considered harmful and hidden trans fats can add up quickly, especially if you eat several servings of multiple foods containing less than 0.5 gram in a serving. It's death by paper cuts. When you check the food label for trans fat, also check the ingredient list for the word "hydrogenated." If it's there, trans fats are too.

Industrial seed oils:

Excessive processing oxidizes seed oils such as canola, corn, cottonseed, soybean, safflower, sunflower, soybean, etc. Rust on steel is a form of oxidization, and these oils are no different. Consuming industrial seed oils is like drinking rusty water.

Step 1: 1L of water per day.

Step 2: Adding a healthy fat to breakfast.

Step 3 is to eat a vegetable with dinner.

Eating vegetables with dinner does two things for us: Decreases systemic inflammation and improves gut health via fiber.

Low-level, chronic inflammation is associated with 7 of the 10 leading causes of mortality. Vegetables are the pound-for-pound king of anti-inflammatory nutrients. If we want to stay alive (let alone Thrive!), we need to eat vegetables.

Vegetables are also the most potent food source of fiber (prebiotics), which act as fertilizer for good bacteria in the gut.

We will eat cooked vegetables with dinner. There are benefits to cooking vegetables as well as to eating them raw, but for the sake of digestion overnight and because most of us like a hot meal for dinner, we’ll save raw vegetables for later down the road.

Cooking vegetables breaks down the plants’ thick cell walls and aids the body’s uptake of some nutrients bound to those cell walls. Two examples are tomatoes and carrots. When to compared to their raw counterparts, cooked tomatoes have 35% more of the antioxidant Lycopene and cooked carrots have increased levels of the antioxidant Beta-carotene. You’ll get similar anti-inflammatory benefits with many other cooked vegetables.

Increased absorption of anti-oxidants and improved gut health before bed will result in a better night’s sleep. A better night’s sleep will result in a more productive day tomorrow, so make it a habit to eat cooked vegetables with dinner every night.

Just like Healthy Fats 101, this discussion of carbs is entirely practical and we’ll save the theoretical for later. I’m not going to advocate for exotic vegetables in this lesson—bok choy is great, but odds are you’re more familiar with broccoli (for those students in the U.S., at least!).

The underlying theme of this course is to add the optimal levels of the foods you should be eating before getting rid of suboptimal foods. Carbs you should eat come from three sources: vegetables, fruit, and starches. We want to minimize or do away with refined sugar and most grains in our kitchens.

1) Vegetables

Vegetables are good for you, and odds are you are not getting enough of them. There’s a pretty easy fix for that: eat more vegetables.

Vegetables are the pound-for-pound king of micronutrient density. They contain large amounts of vitamins, minerals, phytochemicals, and antioxidants.

Green leafy vegetables are predominantly what you eat in salads. Kale, spinach, and romaine lettuce are all great sources of magnesium, fiber, and a broad spectrum of antioxidants. Cruciferous vegetables (i.e. cauliflower, cabbage, bok choy, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, etc.) play an important part in providing fiber. They also detoxify the body in three main ways:
  • Breaking the toxin down and removing it from its location in the body
  • Moving that toxin to the digestive tract to be eliminated
  • Teaming up with fiber to remove toxins from the body
There is no such thing as a bad vegetable, so anything in the grocery store is fair game. That said, avoid canned soup and juices.

See below the list of “clean 15” and “dirty dozen” vegetables to prioritize which vegetables you should spend extra money on for the organic label. The “clean 15” are the top 15 produce items with the least amount of residual pesticides in conventional farming practices; in contrast, the dirty dozen are the 12 produce items with the most residual pesticides from conventional farming.

2) Fruit

Fruit is good for you. The concept that fruit makes people fat is completely misguided. Fruit is a great sources of antioxidants, and incorporating different types of fruit such as berries, tropical varieties, and citrus diversifies your antioxidant profile.

Antioxidants are your cells’ defenders. Different antioxidants protect different cells, so it’s important to vary your antioxidant consumption.

The misconception that fruit is “bad” is the result of what people do with fruit. A prime example is fruit juice. A 12-ounce glass of grapefruit juice requires three to four grapefruits, but no one eats three to four grapefruits in one sitting! Bottled juice has preservatives and is usually spiked with added sugar. Furthermore, juice doesn’t contain any fiber to fertilize the gut or blunt the insulin spike from the excess sugar. In a lot of cases, “juice” is just a sugar water drink with artificial fruit flavoring and a small amount of actual fruit.

The only acceptable way of eating fruit is whole, fresh or frozen. Avoid canned fruit. Canned in syrup or juice often means “in sugar water.”

Good choices are berries: blueberries, raspberries, strawberries, and others. Polyphenolics in berries activate the brain’s natural “housekeepers,” which clean up and recycle biochemical debris that would otherwise get in the way of brain function. Left unchecked, this debris may accelerate age-related memory loss and other mental decline. The polyphenolics in berries not only slow or stop this process, but can also reverse it.

Only buy organic berries, as they’re are one of the most heavily sprayed conventional crops in the world. You can save some money by buying frozen organic berries. I like to buy frozen berries as they are much cheaper.

Citrus—grapefruit, oranges, lemons and limes—is not just for fighting off colds but for recovery from workouts. Citrus is a potent source of intracellular electrolytes magnesium and potassium, which increase cellular hydration after a workout.

Citrus is also the best source of vitamin C, an anti-oxidant that aids in recovery. Training is a stress on the body that creates inflammation. Vitamin C reduces that inflammation, allowing the immune system to focus elsewhere. Reduced inflammation in the body also means fewer stress hormones are produced. It’s a win for everyone.

When shopping for other fruits, opt for organic apples, peaches, nectarines, berries and grapes. Save money and go conventional on pineapples, mangoes, kiwi, grapefruit, and melons.

Avoid juices (aka sugar water), dried fruits that are coated in sugar and/or preservatives, and canned or jarred fruits.

3) Starch

Starches have nutritional value, but their main purpose is fuel. Starch is a slower digesting carbohydrate that produces glucose at a slower rate than sugar, better managing blood sugar for red blood cells.

Potatoes, white, red, yellow, purple, orange—and all the others in-between—have value. Their nutritional profile varies, but they all are good for you. For example, sweet potatoes are high in beta-carotene but white potatoes are high in vitamin B6.

Chris Voigt, the executive director of the Washington State Potato Commission, ate 20 potatoes a day for 60 straight days and lost 20 pounds during that time, all while lowering his cholesterol from 214 to 147. That’s a 31% reduction in 60 days. Now, I’m not recommending you eat 20 potatoes a day for the next 60 days, but it’s important to de-vilify white potatoes.

White rice is basically glucose—a quality source of fuel, cheap, portable, and easy to cook. Be careful to cook your own rice so you don’t get rice made in corn oil or some other industrial seed oil.

One of my favorite ways to eat rice to prepare sushi rice and mix in a splash of rice vinegar and sea salt. The vinegar significantly reduces the insulin response and the salt adds a bit of trace minerals. It also makes a tasty rice dish to eat cold if you don’t want to heat up your lunch.

Squash are both vegetables and starches. Summer squash such as zucchini, yellow squash, and pattypan squash, have a relatively low starch content, but winter squash such as acorn, butternut, and spaghetti are a great source of starch.

Starchy or not, squash are highly nutritious. For instance, winter squashes are among the best plant-based sources of omega-3 (ALA) and beta-carotene. Further, the B vitamins and magnesium in both summer and winter squash aid blood sugar management.

When buying squash, choose summer squash for vegetables, winter squash for starches, and always organic for both.

Gluten-free rolled oats are great, but stay away from the instant varieties. Oats have a low impact on blood sugar due to the high fiber, particularly beta-glucan, which boosts the immune response to infection by neutralizing fungi and bacteria. Avenanthramide is a polyphenol unique to oats that is a potent anti-inflammatory. Incorporated rolled oats into your starch rotation for anti-oxidant diversification.

detailedDesc:
This is the second addition of vegetables. We started with cooked vegetables for dinner, and now you’re going to incorporate raw vegetables into lunch.

Raw vegetables can be tougher to digest because the fiber is intact, but intact fiber is also a benefit of raw vegetables. The nutrients cleaved to fiber can be muted by cooking (for example, Vitamins B and C). By eating both cooked and raw vegetables, you get the full spectrum of nutrients vegetables offer.

In addition to maximizing nutrient absorption, the intact fiber in raw vegetables helps prevent afternoon energy crashes. Fiber slows the digestion of your lunch, stabilizing blood sugar for a 4- to 6-hour window. This will easily get you past the typical late-afternoon energy slump.

Including raw vegetables for lunch can be as simple as a hearty salad, baby carrots, or crudité.

Start adding raw vegetables to your lunch and unleash your afternoon energy.
lesson:
Let’s talk about how to maximize the benefits of protein.

Details matter when it comes to selecting protein sources. Top priority is selecting a protein source with a complete amino acid profile. After that, select proteins that offer extra benefits, such as favorable fatty acid profiles and micronutrients like Vitamin B12. Perhaps even more important than extra nutritional benefits, we should make selections based on the absence of growth hormones, pesticides, and unnecessary additives.

The following proteins all have a complete amino acid profiles, and it’s easy to find quality sources, even in many mainstream markets:

  • Beef
  • Fish and seafood
  • Poultry
  • Lamb
  • Eggs
  • Pork
  • Game meat, when it’s available.

Which protein you eat from the above list is secondary to selecting a protein source based on how the animal was raised and what it was fed. The quality of the animal’s life influences the quality of both its macronutrient and micronutrient profiles.

The closer these animals lived to their natural state, the better. Animals that were 100% grass fed, truly wild caught, or basically allowed to do whatever they do naturally show dramatic benefits compared to animals raised in conventional ways.

1) Beef

You have probably heard more and more about grass-fed beef recently, and for good reason. Most feed lot cows are fed a bioengineered mix of corn, antibiotics, and several growth hormones. Feed lot farming produces beef that is more science experiment than nutrition. The extreme manipulation of the cows’ diet produces meat that isn’t even nutritionally comparable to grass-fed beef. Beef from cattle that were 100% grass fed contains 2 to 4 times the amount of omega-3 fatty acids, is richer in antioxidants, and contains about 5 times more conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), which is the fat toxic to cancer cells.

When eating healthy beef, do not avoid the fattier cuts of meat. In general, grass-fed cows are leaner than corn fed cows (some of the lean cuts are as lean as chicken breast!), but they don’t taste as good as the fattier cuts. Additionally, with leans cuts you are missing out on the main nutritional benefit of grass-fed beef: the omega-3 fat Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

When enjoying fattier cuts of beef from grass-fed cows, you might notice the fat has a yellow tint. This is because grass contains beta carotene, and cows that eat a lot of grass store a lot of beta carotene, which is then passed on to the consumer.

If you don’t have access to grass-fed beef, conventionally raised beef is still a good choice for protein. Conventional beef still offers vitamin B12, selenium, zinc and other B vitamins. When eating conventional beef, avoid the fattier cuts as much as possible.

2) Fish and seafood

: Seafood has the highest-ranked fatty acid profile because it’s low in saturated fat and high in omega-3 fatty acids. To get the most of those omega-3s and other valuable vitamins, look for wild-caught fish. Farm-raised salmon, for example, is much fattier than wild-caught fish, but has about 50% less omega-3s and protein content due to increasing amounts of grain and legume feed. Also, many commercially farmed fish are injected with dyes to give them a more appealing color.

When shopping for fish, note that the term "wild" is nebulous and often misused. In many ways, “wild” similar to the highly abused "natural" designation. Ask your fishmonger where the fish came from. If it's wild, the store will have paid more for it, so they're likely to understand the value proposition. If they don't have an answer for you, that's a red flag that the fish is farmed. Try to avoid Atlantic salmon, as it currently comes from fish farms.

Salmon labeled "Alaskan salmon" is a great choice because there is no farming allowed in Alaska. Another safe option is sockeye salmon, because it cannot be farmed. You can tell sockeye salmon apart from other salmon by its color: it’s bright red as opposed to pale pink

Other options for cold water fish include black cod, Pacific halibut, sea scallops, spiny lobster, and shrimp.

3) Poultry

Poultry such as chicken, turkey, duck, and pheasant boast robust micronutrient profiles:

  • Poultry, and most notably turkey, contains tryptophan, an amino acid that incudes a comforting, sleepy feeling. Tryptophan increases the serotonin levels in your brain, enhances your mood, and helps you sleep.
  • Poultry is a good source of vitamin B6, which is needed for protein metabolism and amino acid synthesis.
  • Chicken is high in phosphorus, an essential mineral that supports your teeth and bones, as well as kidney, liver, and central nervous system function.
  • Chicken is abundant in selenium, an essential mineral involved in metabolic performance—thyroid, hormone, metabolism, and immune function.
  • Chicken is also high in vitamin B6—which promotes methylation, a process that keeps blood vessels healthy, energy levels high, and metabolism burning calories—and niacin, which helps to maintain healthy skin and aids in the digestion and absorption of food.
  • The list goes on, including retinol, alpha and beta-carotene, and lycopene, all derived from vitamin A, which is vital for healthy eyesight.

Birds are omnivores; they eat plants, worms, insects, and bugs. They are not vegetarians, so next time you see “vegetarian fed” on the label, laugh and know that is marketing talk for “fed only grain.” Avoid these poultry products if you can source higher quality poultry products.

Like beef, the lean and fat cuts -- or light and dark meat -- both have benefits. Most dark meats contain more zinc, riboflavin, niacin, thiamin, vitamins B6 and B12, amino acids and iron than white meat.

4) Eggs

Egg are a fat source as much as they are a protein source, so I covered them partially in Healthy Fats 101. I mention them here as well because eggs are one of the best protein sources—they even beat beef in the five main protein quality tests (such as AAS, bioavailability, PER, and PDCAA).

As I mentioned earlier, every protein source mentioned in this lesson has a complete amino acid profile, so the additional nutritional benefits from each source are what really matter as we select protein sources. Eggs come with a lot of additional benefits—even omega-3s like eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA.

detailedDesc:
Now that we have been adding a healthy fat to breakfast for some time, let’s add a protein to it. This is the last item we are going to add to breakfast.

Protein at all meals is important, because your body uses carbs and fats for energy, but needs protein to build and rebuild tissues.

Contractile proteins like your muscles are constantly in a state of rebuilding if you work out, and structural proteins like the elastin in your skin are constantly turning over as well. Aging is how much the process of protein turnover slows down. Getting adequate protein at even intervals throughout the day will slow the aging process.

If you are still eating a handful of macadamia nuts, add some Trader Joe’s beef jerky to it, and you have completed this step.

If you are eating Greek yogurt, congrats. You already have this step completed. There is protein in that yogurt -- whey and casein as a matter of fact, a fast and a slow digesting quality protein.

If you are eating eggs, congrats, too. Eggs have about the best protein score amongst the top 5 protein quality test. Long story short, there are five main ways to determine the quality of protein. Eggs score the highest in all of the five tests.
lesson:
There is nothing sleep doesn’t affect. Body composition (gain/lose), recovery and brain cognition are all directly affected by sleep.

Sleep 7 hours a night. That means lights out, no electronics.

The average person I talk to sleeps about 6 hours a night. Everyone tries to tell me they don’t need any more, but when I take all the coffee and Red Bulls out of their diet, they suddenly begin to sleep more.

  • Coffee to bring you to zero, not ergogenic aid.
  • Survival functions before luxury functions.
  • Handstands are not survival.

This is the most important step to maximize as it is free and has benefits that far exceed any supplement, workout or nutritious meal.

Brain cognition

Just 18 hours of sleep deprivation result in the same reduced performance as a person with a blood alcohol content of .05. If you pull an all-nighter, it’s equivalent to a BAC of .08 to .10. If you go Navy SEAL style and are sleep deprived for longer than four days, your blood sugar and insulin levels mimic those of a diabetic’s.

Our first sleep goal is to sleep 7 hours a night. No distractions.

Good luck.

detailedDesc:
Okay! Step 2 of dinner; Step 1 was adding a vegetable, and now we are adding a protein. Any fresh fish, poultry, or red meat will do.

An animal source of protein is optimal for this. If you are not a meat eater, go for the most complete protein you have available to you.

For a protein source to be complete, it has to contain all nine of the indispensable/essential amino acids. There are actually 20 amino acids, but your body can manufacture the other 11 from the nine essentials.

There are also many “essential” vitamins the body can’t produce that must also be received from food. Vitamin B12 is one of theses vitamins. Vitamin B12 is involved in the function of every cell in the body. It is directly involved in the formation of blood and the function of the brain. A B12 deficiency results in a smaller brain amongst other things -- but that should be enough reason to ensure you’re getting enough of the vitamin.

The only legitimate source of B12 is meat, fish and eggs. The most common nutritional deficiency amongst vegetarians is B12.

The most simplified way to add an animal protein source to dinner is to throw a burger patty in a pan, using a little bit of coconut oil for flavor and so the patty doesn’t stick to the pan. While you have that going, steam some frozen broccoli, and you have completed all of your dinner steps.

Of course if you have time, the sky is the limit.
lesson:
We have talked about the two individual components of breakfast: protein and fat. Now we are going to connect the dots and talk about this meal as a whole.

We aren’t going to add anything else to breakfast; we’re going to stick to a protein source rich in those essential amino acids and a quality fat.

By breakfast you have fasted overnight, somewhere between 10 to 12 hours, depending on when you ate dinner. You go to bed burning the dinner you ate for energy, and you wake up using your own body fat stores for energy.

At some point in the night, your body senses a reduction in glycogen stores and blood sugar, so it begins burning more body fat than carbohydrates for fuel. This allows it to preserve the remaining carbs for the the brain and other body parts that can only run on carbs, while the rest of the body switches over to using body fat as fuel.

By skipping the carbs with breakfast and focusing on a healthy fat and protein, we encourage this process to continue. Effectively, we take the fat-burning window and bust it wide open.

Your body only has two fuel sources, carbs and fat. If we skip the carbs with breakfast, it forces you to burn fat for fuel.

The simple reason why people get fat -- and stay fat -- is because they lose the ability to burn body fat for fuel. This is a serious problem. We need to maintain metabolic flexibility, which is the body’s capability to switch between fat and carbs as a fuel source.

Once you are metabolically flexible, you will be able to bounce back and forth between carbs and fats for energy without effort. All the while you will be in a state of body fat burning. It’s the best of both worlds.

Achieving this new equilibrium could take your body up to six weeks.

Just keep working at it and it will happen.

detailedDesc:
This is the third and final meal you will be adding protein to.

Why protein first?

Because if you could only eat one macronutrient, it’s the one you would live the longest on. Eating protein at all three meals is important because the more protein you consume, the more protein you will synthesize; and the more you synthesize, the more proteins you will turn over. You are constantly turning over proteins in every part of your body, from your eyes to your toes. The more proteins you have to replace old or damaged ones, the more optimal your health will be.

One thing I never covered in Protein 101 is that your immune health is closely tied to how much protein you consume. The immune system requires protein for proper T-cell function. T-cells are your active germ fighters; they have X-ray vision and can see inside cells to root out problems. The immune system requirement is only increased the more you train.

An easy option is to just to have some leftovers from last night or toss some sliced-up chicken on a salad.
lesson:
The purpose of this step is to set yourself up for success. By having the right food in your house it gives you the option to eat the right things. Further, if you minimize the junk, you reduce or eliminate the ability to make the wrong decision.

When you make room for the good stuff it makes it easy to get rid of the crap.

These are a few pictures and a list of the things my family keeps in our fridge.

But first lets address some things that aren’t in my fridge! We don’t keep quasi healthy junk food around, we don’t bend the “paleo” rules to make brownies or cookies or any other crap. Fact of the matter is date paste is pure fructose, you would be better off just using sugar as it has a lower fructose content and tastes way better. Coconut flour is almost as high as regular flour in anti-nutrients. This is why all of my programs include a day off - just go out and get the real thing and get it over with so we can get back to business.

We try to shop small and more frequently. I personally don’t like to commit to what I am going to eat for Thursday night dinner on Sunday. We go shopping(me, my wife and my son) on Sunday and Wednesday. We are also very selective of what we buy in bulk. For example: a 5 pound bag of potatoes would go bad before we ever ate them. The secret to keeping the grocery bill down is to be selective in this way. Wasted food from cooking too much or buying too much and it rotting is the number one reason grocery bills spike. Eating is like getting dressed, yea this shirt may be your favorite but you want to wear your other shirt today because you feel you look good in it. Shopping 1x a week or less is like picking out what you are going to wear next Friday. Buy small and and pick the things that look good to you at that time.

Items we buy in bulk:

  • coconut oil
  • butter
  • beef
  • fish
  • rice
  • and frozen berries

Fridge

Most refrigerators have several compartments that serve unique purposes as well as temperature zones. Taking advantage of these features can lead to less waste and crisper greens overall saving you from making poor choices.

Lets work top to bottom to keep it simple.

  • Upper shelves are reserved for Leftovers, drinks, ready to eat foods, and fresh herbs.
  • Middle/Lower Shelves are for eggs, dairy, and raw meat.
  • Crisper is for Fruits and Veggies. Good tip here is to keep these separate if possible. Do you actually know how to set the crisper or humidity drawers in your fridge?
  • Most humidity drawers are adjustable between low and high. These settings simply open or close a window in the drawer. The low humidity setting the window is completely open and the high humidity setting it is completely closed. Here are two basic principles that can save your lettuce!

The general rule of thumb is to put things that tend to rot in a drawer with a low humidity setting. This includes fruits and veggies that emit an ethylene gas, like apples and pears, because leaving the window open on the drawer gives those gases a chance to escape. When the gases are released, it helps keep the fruits and vegetables from rotting prematurely.

Here are some common fruits and vegetables to keep in this drawer:

  • apples
  • avocados
  • cantaloupes
  • honeydews
  • kiwis
  • mangoes
  • papayas
  • pears
  • plantains
  • stone fruits (apricots, nectarines, peaches, plums)

Things that wilt in the high humidity drawer. This will be all your leafy greens like arugula, spinach, and kale. By having the window closed, water vapor is held in the drawer and the moisture keeps the greens crisper and fresher longer. Keeping fruits and vegetables that are sensitive to ethylene gas, like strawberries, in this drawer will also keep them away from ethylene producers.

Here are some common fruits and vegetables to keep in this drawer:
  • broccoli
  • Brussels sprouts
  • cabbage
  • carrots
  • cauliflower
  • cucumbers
  • eggplant
  • green beans
  • leafy greens (kale, lettuces, spinach, Swiss chard, watercress)
  • okra
  • peas
  • peppers
  • strawberries
  • watermelon

Even organic food gets dirty so you want to wash your food before eating but too much moisture can cause foods to go from ripe to rotten faster than you can eat them. The goal is to wash fruits and veggies when it’s convenient, but not so far in advance that they are likely to spoil before you eat them. When washing fruits, remove extra moisture by draining in a colander, blotting with paper towel, or using a salad spinner. Berries are particularly fragile, so eat them within a day or two of washing.

As you prepare your greens and herbs place in a plastic bag or container with a square of paper towel to soak up excess moisture. Best place to then store them is on the top shelf where you’re more likely to see them and eat them up quickly.

Doors

Doors are the warmest part of the fridge. These are reserved for condiments and other foods that can stand up to temperature fluctuations here. Optional items here could be butters or oils.

Now lets talk about the actual ingredients in the fridge.

Fresh herbs

Always try to keep a few fresh herbs on hand, you can pretty much put them on anything. basil, thyme, rosemary, cilantro are the go-to’s in our house. But there are many more out there to chose from.

Vegetables

Salad fixings ( spinach, kale, mixed greens) should be a staple item to have in the fridge. You can alternate in-between types of greens and toppings as well. Buy some spinach and put some cucumbers and tomatoes in the mix, then next time go for spinach with a little bit of cabbage and carrots. Keep changing it up. You should also have 1-2 fresh veggies on hand for cooking with dinner like brussels sprouts, they are one of the ones that don’t come out as well frozen.

Fruit

Lemon or lime is great to keep around if you drink sparkling water(no, lime flavored water, it is not the same thing). When berries are in season they are a must and depending on if your much of a fruit eater then a easy to pack around fruit like an apple or two is also nice to have.

Meat and fish

Given that you have some reserve(in the freezer) you only need what you are going to eat for tonight’s meat and tomorrow’s in the fridge. This gives you good flexibility. If you accidentally run out of meat you always have a can of tuna in the pantry. A dozen eggs are also good to have in the fridge too.

Dairy

Again if dairy isn’t for you just skip over this part. The nice thing about fermented dairy is it lasts along time. Keeping a Keifer in the fridge for a back up will last a long time. A grass fed cheese is nice to throw on eggs. Greek Yogurt is quick and easy and heavy cream is nice in the coffee from time to time.

Butter

grass-fed unsalted butter is the way to go, you can find it just about anywhere. You want unsalted because they add a low quality salt with no mineral content and you also want to be able to adjust your own salt level.

Ghee

This is the way to go if you are dairy intolerant. Ghee is pretty much butter with the lactose, casein and whey removed. A majority of the nutrients are still there as they reside in the fat.

Condiments

  • Djon,
  • olives,
  • capers,
  • garlic,
  • Sriracha,
  • Franks red hot,
  • sauerkraut,
  • local/fresh pickles.

Freezer

The trick with freezers is to keep things well organized and tightly in their containers. Think of you freezer as insurance…you can have extra meat, vegetables, stocks, and you may even get crazy and have extra prepared meals ready to go in the freezer too just in case you get into a bind. But lets not get ahead of ourselves. What are the basics?

If you can it is a good idea to keep a grass fed cow in the freezer. You can save a ton of money that way. By far and away the thing we use out of the freezer the most is the frozen berries, considerably cheeper and in the months they are out of season you are still getting quality berries. Frozen “wild” fish is a good one to have around as well.

Vegetables

We go for the medleys or mixes because we aren’t going to cut up 3 veggies and steam and eat them so when its frozen we like to mix it up. Another good way to go is the high prep work stuff is nice to get frozen, squash would be a good example.

Meat

We buy a 1/4 cow at a time, we can eat this before it starts getting freezer burn and we tend to give some away to clients and friends who are unaware of the difference. We’ve done a 1/2 lamb and pig as well but prefer the beef, we also like to keep a whole fish in there. Some cocktail shrimp are great and thaw easy to put on salads for lunch.

Pantry

Cooking Oils/Fats: Olive oil, avocado, or coconut oil.

Vinegars

Balsamic vinegar is great but real balsamic vinegar is expensive, very expensive. The fake stuff is just sugar water with a grape flavor, so opt for the real stuff it will go a long way and the taste is better too! Apple cider vinegar isn’t frequently used but it can go good on Brussels sprouts at times, rice vinegar is another nice choice as it gives rice a good flavor profile and it lowers the insulin response to the rice.

Nuts

Try to buy is slightly smaller quantities and try to keep getting fresh ones. Macadamia nuts are your best choice. Whatever you do don't buy out of the bulk bins, who knows what dirty bird put their nasty paw in there and they are usually really old nuts. Don't get caught cracking out on the flavored or honey covered nuts either.

Spice rack

A good 50% of the time we are just seasoning our food with a sea salt and cracked peeper. You would be amazed what a high quality meat cooked perfectly with a bit of salt and pepper on it can taste like. We like to keep no more than about 10 spices in the house. Sometimes we have a beef, poultry, and or fish rub but right now we only have the chicken rub. But the got-to’s for us are:

10 go to spices.

  • Sea Salt
  • Pepper
  • Cumin
  • Paprika
  • Cayenne
  • Cinnamon
  • Herbs Providence
  • Chili Powder
  • Chili Flakes
  • Vanilla extract (high quality like Madagascar)

What we don’t have in our house: Fake health foods! Coconut, arrowroot, tapioca flower. We don’t have agave nectar, sugar, molasses, date paste or any form of sweetener. Could the argument be made that pure local honey is far more nutritious than plain white sugar? Yes and it is. But keep that stuff out of your house. Trust me on this one, you are better off just going out and getting the real thing once a week and properly quenching your craving then getting back to business.

Okay guys this is a ton of information and its all the practical stuff my family does. We love french food and our kitchen has that slant, pick your own direction and go for it. The real trick to all this is making it your own. Steal ideas from me and come up with new ones. Get some practice at this now, in level 2 your kitchen needs to be on point.

detailedDesc:
I said carbs are a double-edged sword; here is the other edge. It’s pretty hard to eat too much kale, but it’s not nearly as difficult to eat too much rice.

Starches and fats are the “energy” in your diet. Starches are going to turn into glucose once digested and top off glycogen stores in your muscles. There are a few specific parts of the brain that can only use glycogen and the red blood cells require glycogen as well.

A potato or rice are good starches to add to dinner.

It’s dinner time, which means you are going to be going to bed shortly. Adding a starch to your evening meal will do two things: 1) It will get you producing some serotonin to prepare for the sleep to come, and 2) It will help with recovery from your GST session.

About 90% of the serotonin in your body is produced in your gut. Eating a dinner with some starches in it will get your insulin levels to go up. Insulin will push the amino acids from the proteins you are eating into your muscles, except for the amino acid tryptophan (the one concentrated in turkey). When tryptophan is the only amino acid in the bloodstream, it doesn’t have to compete with the others to get into your brain. It’s the tryptophan that actually makes you sleepy.

Recovering from your GST session requires your insulin stores to rebuild after transferring amino acids to your muscles, and some glycogen in those muscles for their energy to rebuild.

Best evening sources of glycogen

  • Most Favorable: Squashes, sweet potatoes, regular potatoes, yams, white rice, jasmine, wild rice (not actually rice), yuca, taro, plantain.
  • Least Favorable: Most grains and legumes.
  • Unfavorable: Gluten, packaged, processed.
lesson:
Today we are going to talk about the gut and how digestion actually happens.

The primary purpose of the digestive system is to break down the foods you eat into forms that the body can absorb and distribute for energy. The digestive system also has two other important functions: shield the body from foreign invaders, and remove waste.

The digestive system is part of the gut. The gut isn’t just the digestive tube itself but the living organisms inside the gut, intestinal flora, and the immune and nervous systems within and around the walls of the intestine. The body doesn’t make a distinction between these parts, and neither should we.

The gut is comprised of four components that act in harmony like an orchestra. These components require full team work for optimal digestion. They are the nervous system (in your head and your gut), the digestive tube itself (the stomach and the small and large intestines), gut flora (beneficial bacteria in the gut), and the immune system.

Nervous system

This is the software that tells the hardware what to do. Digestion begins in the brain; your state of mind is what sets the foundation for optimal digestion. When you are in the “rest and digest” state of mind vs. “fight or flight” mode, your body naturally increases blood flow to the gut to aid in digestion, motility to stretch and contract gut muscles as well as enzyme production to break down food.

Digestive system

If the nervous system is the software, then the digestive tube is the hardware. The digestive tube itself starts with your mouth, then travels through the esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, before it ends at the toilet. It’s the 20- to 30-foot path that the food you eat actually travels. Digestion begins in your mouth, where the first mechanical step occurs: chewing, breaking down the food and mixing it with saliva. Then the food travels down through the esophagus to the stomach.

The stomach’s main purpose is to break down and disassemble the food we consume. The stomach also does a good job cleaning the food. Its acidity level is somewhere near that of battery acid. This helps in killing unwanted germs and breaking down our food for the small intestines.

After the stomach completes a majority of the digestion, the food travels to the small intestine, where most of the absorption into the body takes place. The small intestine has multiple folds on top of folds. This increases the surface area so that food can be absorbed with maximum efficiency. If you were to iron out all the folds of the small intestine, it would be the size of a tennis court.

Then it’s off to the large intestine. The most metabolically active organ in the human body, the large intestine contains numerous and diverse species of gut flora or bacteria. The large intestine can ferment carbohydrates such as fibers and sugars that the body failed to digest and or absorb. It turns them into short-chain fatty acids, which are used in the body as energy.

Quick review

The nervous system is the software. The digestive tube -- mouth, stomach and intestines -- is the hardware. This is where the beneficial bugs, the gut flora, hang out.

Gut flora

The bacteria that reside in your digestive tract are building blocks for the immune system. The flora in your gut does not share your DNA, but they may as well be considered part of you. Gathered together, the flora in your gut alone are approximately the size of a football. If they were turned into an organ, it would be one of the biggest in your body. The heath and variety of these bugs is dictated by the foods you eat. They aid in digestion, provide nutrients and even help with immunity to some illnesses by inhibiting certain pathogens before they ever reach the immune system. The gut flora are the protectors of our intestines. They fight to protect their territory as well as help the immune system ward off bad pathogens from entering the body.

Gut flora live on the inside of the intestinal wall, behind enemy lines if you will. On the other side of the intestinal wall is the immune system -- 80% of it as a matter of fact. This makes your intestines the front lines for contact with pathogenic microorganisms. Your intestinal wall can be damaged just like your skin, and a healthy immune system is needed to help plug the hole. Think of the intestinal wall like a brick wall. However tightly the bricks are packed together is how healthy your intestinal wall is.

The immune system is wrapped around the digestive tube and the nervous system is wrapped around the immune system. Think of this like your second brain. In total weight, the nervous system in your gut is heavier than the nervous system in your head. It also produces the same neurotransmitters than the brain does. Of particular interest is the neurotransmitter serotonin, 90% of which is produced in your gut, not your brain.

The nervous system in the gut and in the brain are in constant communication and management of the rest of the body. The foods you eat directly affect the messages the nervous system in your gut sends to the nervous system in your head -- just another reason why nutrition is so important.

Now we know the four layers of the gut and their specific function. Remember, digestion starts in your brain with your state of mind -- “rest and digest.” After you chew your food, it’s off to your stomach, then the small intestine for absorption, where it will meet the first of many gut flora. It’s the job of that flora and the intestinal wall to keep the bad out and let the good in. On the other side of that wall is the immune system to make sure nothing bad got in. If it did, it’s the immune system’s job is to deal with it. Around the immune system is the nervous system, your second brain, controlling the orchestra of digestion and sending and receiving signals from the brain.

Alright, guys, that was a lot of information. Be sure to review the notes below and feel free to listen to this a second time.
Cheers.

detailedDesc:
We have added a fat to breakfast, and now we will add one to lunch. The whole goal of lunch is to eat a meal that is nutrient-dense AND does a good job of managing blood sugar late into the day. We want to avoid the 2pm drop in energy.

Fat is twice as dense as protein or carbohydrate per gram. It also takes longer to break down and absorb. This gives you a slow and steady energy source.

Per unit, fat produces twice the energy carbs do. It does this by recycling energy with less waste than carbs. The only downside is that fat takes considerably longer, but in this case it’s actually a benefit BECAUSE we are trying to avoid that 2pm drop in energy.

Adding fat to lunch can be as easy as adding a quarter or half of an avocado to what you already eat. It can be as elaborate as having some salmon and avocado sushi.

Please try to avoid using nuts.

Nuts are good for you, but not great. Keep them for for when you are in a time crunch.

Other great sources of fat are olive oil on your salad, olives, or a fermented or aged cheese like a quality aged cheddar or blue cheese (full fat on all dairy products).
lesson:
Dinner is all about setting yourself up for rest and recovery. The day is over and so is the workout. Now it’s time to prepare for tomorrow.

We want to recover from our training session and set ourselves up for a good night’s sleep. We’re already putting in the time, so let’s make sure we get the most out of it.

How we maximize recovery and set ourselves up to get the most out of our sleep is to eat a nutrient-dense meal with optimal amounts of protein, fat, carbs and micronutrients.

Your body is not dormant when you’re sleeping. You are burning just slightly less energy than sitting on the couch watching a movie. During sleep is when your body’s construction workers, house cleaners and maintenance men come out. We want to give them the supplies they need to get the job done.

antioxidants

Think of antioxidants as your brain’s house cleaners during sleep. While your brain is resting, the cleaners come in armed with antioxidants and micronutrients to straighten things up and take out the neural trash.

Proteins

Proteins are your body’s construction workers. Sleep is their time to build more efficient muscle or rebuild damaged skin, as well as a hundred other things.

carbs and fats

Your carbs and fats are your maintenance crew. They go around reloading tissues with glycogen and fat-soluble vitamins. This is the same process your body goes through for recovery from a workout.

It doesn’t matter if you trained today or not. Recovery is a multi-day process and needs to be a daily practice. A complete protein and starch is how we nutritionally recover.

Okay, guys, now let’s address eating before sleeping. It’s totally bunk that you shouldn’t eat before bed. And more specifically, it is nonsense that you shouldn’t eat carbs before bed. As a matter of fact, eating a mixed meal 1 to 3 hours before bed is optimal for body composition, recover and quality of sleep.

Eating some carbs with dinner is proven to help you get to sleep faster and reduce stress levels. So don’t be afraid of carbs with dinner.

Good luck.

detailedDesc:
It’s lunch time.

We have added a raw vegetable, protein and fat, and now we’re adding a starch to make lunch a complete meal.

If you are in a bind, you can substitute a piece of fruit or two for carbs, but there are plenty of sources of starches out there. Sweet potatoes, regular potatoes, various squashes and rices are some examples. Further down the road, Ezekiel bread will be an option, but not yet.

Carbs are the preferential fuel source for the body. What that means is when carbs are present in the body, they will get used first. Eating a meal containing carbs before you work out provides energy for that training session.

Carbs also provide some “now” energy. Combined with the rest of your lunch, this covers all your bases to keep energy up through the rest of the day with no after-lunch dip.

On a side note

By comparison, starches do have a lower nutritional content than vegetables. Everything does. You shouldn’t be relying on them exclusively for nutrients, however. They taste good, and they are a good, clean source of energy. One thing most nutrition books fail to cover is mental health. Adding a controlled amount of starch with lunch and dinner is not only optimal for health, but it makes nutrition so much more enjoyable and less like work.

!! A very low-carbohydrate diet over a long-term period significantly decreases protein synthesis in the muscles. !!

Good luck with your first complete meal!
lesson:
Intro

It’s a myth that fat is the cause of disease and obesity. The reality is, fat -- including saturated fat -- has benefits to health. Refined sugars and grains play a larger role in health problems such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer due to their extreme effect on insulin/blood sugar.

It is a natural assumption that eating fat makes you fat and eating cholesterol raises your cholesterol.

But in actuality:

  • Your body makes 75% of the cholesterol in your blood. Only 25% comes from food. So the real question is, what causes the body to make too much cholesterol? The short answer: Refined sugars and grains.
  • Just like cholesterol, the fat you eat is not the same as the fat on your body. The fat you eat is an energy source. It’s the refined sugars and grains you eat that more readily convert to body fat.

Low fat is a religion, not a science.

In the United States, the war against fat started when President Dwight Eisenhower became obsessed with his cholesterol because of his heart attacks. Despite following a low-fat diet, his cholesterol, heart problems and weight kept rising.

This was followed up by scientist Ancel Keys’ research, which was the driving force behind the hypothesis that eating fat equals heart attack risk. He was convinced that eating fat of any kind would raise cholesterol, and high cholesterol causes heart disease. His famous Seven Countries Study was his proof. The problem was, he studied 22 countries and picked the seven that would support his hypothesis that eating fat was the driving force behind heart disease.

Nevertheless, in 1977 Senator George McGovern announced the Dietary Goals for the United States based off Keys’ research: a diet made up of 60% carbohydrate and 30% fat. This was during the time when butter was replaced by margarine, more refined sugar was added to the diet, and real food was replaced by processed, artificial food. All to meet the new Dietary Goals.

That is the short story where fat got its bad name.

But not all fat is bad, and there are benefits of incorporating healthy fats into your diet. Healthy fats contain essential nutrients for life. Fat is the major nutrient needed by our brain and nervous system. Fat also forms our cell membranes. The types of fat you consume dictate how well those cell membranes will function. Fat is also responsible for the absorption, transportation and function of vitamins A, D, E and K. Finally, healthy fats provide your body with a clean energy source.

Fat is the major nutrient in your brain. Your brain is approximately 60% fat. It has the highest density of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid, or DHA. DHA creates myelin, the white matter that wraps neural circuits. The more myelin that wraps a circuit, the faster and stronger it will fire, resulting in improved skill acquisition and learning.

Cell membranes in the body are made of fats. Membranes made from healthy fats are more fluid-like and attract nutrients as well as oxygen for use. Unhealthy fats are like concrete walls; nothing can get into the cell.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are known as fat soluble vitamins and require fats for absorption in the gut, transportation from the gut to the part of the body where they are needed. These are the vitamins that assist protein in keeping your immune system running. Fats are responsible for their proper functioning.

For optimal nutrition:

  • It is important that you incorporate beneficial sources of fat and decreasing the disadvantageous sources.
  • Omega-3 fatty acids are the best of what fat has to offer, as well as the hardest to come by. They should be prioritized. Eating cold-water fish 2 to 3 times per week is ideal, as these fish are among the top sources for omega-3s.

Alright, guys! Keep drinking that water and make sure you incorporate one of these healthy fats with breakfast.

detailedDesc:
Time for water goal #2.

Every day you have been drinking a liter of water. It should feel pretty normal by now, and it shouldn’t take much effort to get that L down.

Step 2

Men are going to add another 1L, and ladies 0.5L. For all but the most active, this is all the water you will need to get through your day. This last water goal is to counteract all the water loss we experience through the day.

You lose water through noticeable actions like sweating from exercise, feces and urine.

We also lose water in unnoticed ways. Our lungs are “wet” and when we breathe in, water in our lungs humidifies that air. We lose that water when we breath out. Our skin also loses water through evaporation. We can lose somewhere between half a liter to a full liter of water per day from just these two unnoticed processes.

From here on out you can also measure your hydration by urine color. Clear or lightish yellow means you are hydrated; dark yellow means it’s time to drink some water.

The water goal is the minimum. It’s up to you to be a thinking shooter and adjust based on circumstances. Keep yourself in the clear (or light yellow) even if that means drinking a little more on some days.
lesson:
Alright, guys, it’s lunch time. This should be the first carbs you eat today. If you go any longer without carbs, you will start to get brain fog and low energy.

Low carb meals have their benefits, but we’ve maximized those benefits. Now it’s time to move on. All good things must come to an end.

At a certain point of “no carb” eating, protein synthesis and efficiency plummet. We want to throw some starches in the mix to make sure this does not happen. These starches are also going to double as our training session fuel.

Lunch will be our only meal containing all four components:

  • starch
  • vegetables,
  • fat
  • and protein.

Protein

Protein is there because your body is constantly rebuilding and replacing old proteins. The more efficiently you turn protein over, the more optimal your health.

Vegetables

Vegetables are the primary source of micronutrients and fiber.

Fat

Fat provides us with a slow and steady energy source. When we are not working out, we want to be using fats for energy, as they burn cleaner over the long term and being a good fat burner means we burn more body fat.

We are at the halfway point in your day, so there is an important role for each of the four components. Quick energy for training, slow energy to keep you going, micronutrients and protein.

Alright, guys, after lunch is the time of day where you have your best coordination, fastest reaction times and you’re at your strongest.

It’s a good time to work out! Good luck.

description: 1+ fist size portions of vegetables with dinner
detailedDesc:
More important than anything is eating the right foods, and that’s what we’ve focused on up until this point: Quality first. Vegetables, healthy fats and proteins. You can get really far eating the right foods in the wrong proportions when you pack in that many nutrients.

But good is the enemy of the great! We want to thrive, not survive.

Next step

The next step we are going to take is dialing in the portion sizes at our meals, to ensure getting the optimal amount of nutrients. We are going to do this from a pragmatic, realist approach. We are not going to use a scale or measuring cups. We are going to use our hands. Yep, our hands. This is the “failure is not an option” approach.

When you go out to dinner with friends, are you going to bring a scale or some other measuring device? No. But you are going to bring your hands.

This is a pretty clever way to measure your food because the bigger you are, the bigger your hands are, the bigger the serving size. For dinner, I want you to eat 1 to 2 fist-sized portions of vegetables. Any more, and it may be hard to get the rest of the meal down.

So let’s see what that looks like. [Practical example]

One or two fistfuls of lightly cooked vegetables with dinner. A really quick tip: Vegetables are different colors because they have different antioxidant profiles. Next time you go to the store, try to pick a color you haven’t eaten in a while.
lesson:
If you intend to be “heathy” you need to learn how to cook. Acknowledge, accept and move on. To cook you first need groceries. I am going to show you how to shop and send you off with some materials for the grocery store. Below are the fundamentals of how to shop for foods and I added in some of our personal favorite stuff. You are welcome to do what we do or go in your own direction just as long as you are using the principals below.

There is some overlap here with bulletproof your kitchen. Feel free to go back and refresh yourself on that information.

There are a number of places to buy food. They range dramatically in price and quality. Buying foods from a real farmer(not some joker at the farmers market with a box of grocery store produce) is about the best way to get quality. Take notice however; if what they are offering is in season. A real farmer will show up with a limited supply of seasonal product. Where as a grocery store rarely runs out but the quality is not as high. Ideally you will have a mixture of the two. You will have to do some leg work to find a legitimate source of locally farmed produce, fruit, grass fed cows, and eggs(#1 thing to find locally). There are many cases when the local farmers are out of supply, you will have the grocery store as a backup. The possibilities with buying from local sources are endless and you’ll find the more you seek out the better quality you find and the more knowledgeable you become about the quality of your food.

The below is a guide to help you navigate through the grocery store and get you on your way to cooking and eating quality food.

Produce Section

Basically contains your vegetables, starches(excluding rice) and fruits. The key to produce is knowing which ones to buy organic and which ones to save the money on. Generally speaking if it has a thin skin and it’s exposed (strawberry) it needs to be organic as the pesticides penetrate the skin easily. Things like a coconut is far less concerning. Here is the EWG.org “Dirty Dozen” and “Clean 15” based on their research these are the 12 fruits/vegetables that you must buy organic and the 15 that you can get away with not going organic on.

Vegetables

You pretty much can’t go wrong here, just pick something and eat it. In the downloadable PDF I have listed them out for you but feel free to experiment with vegetables that aren’t on the list.

Fruit

Think seasonal on this one. If the berries aren’t looking good or the price is outrageous go for the frozen ones.

Meat

At the grocery store the best your going to get is “Grass fed” which means fed anywhere from one blade of grass to a decent amount but more than likely these cows(and lamb) were not fed exclusively grass. “Grass fed” is a middle ground, and still a good choice. You aren’t going to get real pasture raised chickens at the grocery store, but you can still get some good quality meats. Here is a food quality guide for when buying eggs and poultry:

Dairy

This can be a slippery slope for a lot of people and if it doesn’t agree with you don’t force it. But if it does then here is what you need to consider when buying

  • 1) It has to be full fat - This is a deal breaker.
  • 2) Ideally fermented-It is a more nutrient dense choice
  • 3) It is nice to have from grass fed cows, raw, and organic. Keifer, greek yogurt, heavy cream and aged cheeses. Real cheese comes in a wheel coated in wax, this is how you know it was aged. When you are at the store you are looking for wedges of cheese. If its shredded or in singles, spreadable or anything else it is not real cheese.

Fats and Oils

Apply all the same principals of “meats” to animal sources of fat. I know butter is technically dairy but I am going to use it for my example here; grass fed butter is better than regular butter; just like 100% grass-fed is higher quality meat. For oils, they don’t have a long shelf life(excluding coconut oil) before they start going backwards in nutrients. You ideally want as fresh as you can get, extra virgin ensure the oil came from a fresh quality olive(in the case of olive oil) and you ideally want organic because oil is a concentrated form of the nut, seed, or fruit in which it came and you don’t want a concentrated source of pesticides.

Nuts

Another slippery slope here, the bargain nuts make look like a great deal but as with even packaged nuts it is virtually impossible to know how old the nuts are, where they were stored, mold levels and so on. Further, as you know there is nothing besides convince that is really all that outstanding about nuts. With that said; opt for a dry roasted or raw nut. You really don’t want any form of peanut oil or any other kind of oil on them.

Beverages

Water and water alone counts towards your water goal. But, that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy other beverages. I am not a fan of liquid calories, I am a fan of liquids that contain nutrients though. One exception to my rule is Keifer. If you have ever drank it, you know, its quite filling; just remember to look for full fat. I also enjoy a Pellegrino sparkling water with a fresh slice of lemon or lime. Some other common beverages are variations of green, black and herbal tea; there is literally a thousand options. It can be expensive but try a tin of matcha green tea powder. I put about a spoonful in a glass and mix it up. Be careful its strong, you may get a DUI at that level of antioxidants. Another option is coffee; if the beans are shinny then they are burnt and some or all of the nutrients are gone. This is another one of those things you want fresh and organic. It’s great to find a local roaster for your coffee beans as well.

Herbs and Spices

These are possibly the trickiest of all things to get right. Many of the spices you find in the spice isle are actually made from very low quality on the verge of rotting herbs. Quality spices are very expensive, but they also go a very long way. When you are looking for a herb you want it to be the only thing listed under the ingredients, don’t believe the misleading information about “anti-caking” agents and all that.

Find ones that say: NO gluten or any kind of wheat, MSG, artificially coloring(tip that they stated with a low quality ingredient), preservatives, sugar(yes, a majority of spices have HFCS in them), irradiation(zaps every nutrient, gone!) peanuts, soy, tree nuts.

See what I mean about this is a tricky one! I would recommend going online and look for a legitimate spice company. You will pay more for higher quality here but it’s worth it. What you will notice is how much more potent the flavor is. A container of real paprika(my fav on eggs) will last you a long, long time.

You do not need a lot of spices: Our go to’s are Salt and Pepper half the time. Try to keep less than 10 spices in the house, this ensures you are rotating them and they don’t sit there for 5 years before you use them.

Quick Reminder

Heathy junk food is a waste of time. Don’t try to concoct a pie with ingredients that at one point were considered heathy. No flours, heathy sugars or any of that nonsense. You are doing yourself more of a favor just going out on your day off and getting a desert. Don’t keep the stuff in the house!

Okay guys download the shopping list and use this and bulletproof your kitchen as a reference for any questions you have. Also, you can ask me questions directly on the forum.
