description: 1+ fist size portions of vegetables with lunch
detailedDesc:
We are back. This is the second edition of portion sizes and the second and last edition of vegetables. We are going to add the exact same portion size of vegetables to lunch as we did dinner.

Quick reminder: Dinner is cooked vegetables and lunch is raw vegetables.

This is going to be easy.

[Example] Spinach, a couple of cherry tomatoes, olive oil and some lemon.

Now that we have vegetables at lunch and dinner, AND portion minimums to meet, poor gut health can’t hide. You may have trouble stomaching all of these veggies, and if you do, it’s not because you are not allergic to vegetables! Trust me. Haha! You’re not.

It’s because the machinery in your gut isn’t operating at 100%. Your gut adapts to whatever you feed it, and if you have been feeding it potato chips it’s not going to like all these vegetables at first.

The good news is your gut is resilient. It can be radically changed by just eliminating refined sugar and grains. The entire body is extremely resilient and can bounce back from a whole lot of damage. All you have to do is give it the time and stay the course.
lesson:
By now, you have the individual meals down pretty well, but let’s take a step back and look at this from a distance. We are going to briefly start with dinner of the day before, then run all the way through dinner of the next day.

The reason I want to take a moment to step back is because I want you to see what you have working for yourself. We have the best of both worlds: fat loss and muscle performance.

No matter your body composition, we’re always after fat loss. We always want to be burning our own body fat for energy. After you’re lean, this applies to health more than anything. There is never a point where fat burning and body composition isn’t on the front of your mind when you are thinking about health and nutrition.

Performance is equally important. Your training session is a very hard but very short portion of the day. The other 90% is recovery and rebuilding from that training session. Progress day by day, year over year in the gym is a direct reflection of your nutrition.

Our whole plan is centered around these two points. Maximize fat utilization for fuel and improved performance.

Your dinner consists of a starch, vegetables, protein and some fat. The purpose behind this is rest and recovery. We want to give your body everything it needs for optimal sleep and restoration.

At some point in the night, your body realizes it’s running low on carbs and starts shifting over to body fat for fuel. This is the beginning of the no-carb window. The great thing about this is that you are sleeping, making this half of your no-carb window really easy.

When you wake up, we keep the fat burning train rolling with a protein and fat breakfast. Your body used its protein from dinner to repair and replace things during your sleep, so it’s time to add some more. Fat is our source of energy and nutrients.

This also keeps your body sparing carbs for things that can only run on glucose, shifting everything else over to fat. This is beneficial because we are burning off body fat and improving your carb utilization efficiency. Basically, you need fewer carbs to create more energy.

This also sets you up for the best morning mental performance. In the morning, we want to increase drive, motivation and clarity of thought. The neurotransmitter dopamine is responsible for this. Our fat and protein breakfast will boost dopamine, effectively stopping the coffee dependency before it starts. The coffee and sugar addiction pathway relies heavily on low dopamine.

In the very early morning, your sleeping cortisol rises. This is responsible for waking you up and keeping you up in the early morning. Cortisol also frees energy stores in the body to be burned for fuel. Your body naturally wants to burn fat at this time of the day. The opposing hormone insulin, which is related to fat storage, is at its lowest in the morning. You are naturally set up to burn body fat in the morning. We just want to encourage it.

Starting your day with quality fats and proteins effectively doubles or triples your fat burning, while feeding your body all the nutrients it needs in optimal doses.

At lunch, you’re going to be eating a little bit of everything. Starches are needed at this point to preserve muscle mass and ensure optimal brain function. Fats still provide some energy, and it really helps in balancing blood sugar along with fiber. When we go into the training session we want to have everything working for us.

Dinner serves as your post-workout refuel, topping off nutrient stores for the muscles and nervous system. This also helps serotonin production start for the evening to aid in relaxation and sleep.

Just eating nutritious food isn’t enough. If you want to push the limits of health and performance, you need to apply everything you know to stack the deck in your favor.

Optimized sleep and nutrient timing as it relates to both health and performance leads to maximum fat burning and recovery, higher vitamin, mineral and probiotic status, and balanced blood sugar, neurotransmitter and hormone levels. Layer all that with the right training program, and you have everything working for you.

description: 1+ (2 Max) palm size portions of animal protein with dinner
detailedDesc:
Okay, we’ve portioned up vegetables, which sometimes leaves less room in your stomach for the other things. Protein should not be one of those things.

Like with the vegetables, we are going to use our hands to select our portion sizes for protein. This time, instead of using a fist, we are going to use our palm or an open hand.

[Example] a protein that is palm-sized and one that is hand-sized.

It’s important to meet this protein minimum because the body only stores protein in your muscles. They get catabolized to produce the proteins needed for things like your immune system, unless you’re getting new protein from your meals. In the name of progress in the gym, eat your protein.

As your plate fills up, it naturally leaves less and less room for sub-optimal foods -- which is what we are after. If we fill our plate up with proper amounts of quality foods, the amount of “junk” food is so limited that it naturally falls within acceptable range.
lesson:
Alright, guys, we are going to talk about carbs. As far as we are concerned, carbs fall into one of three categories:

  • vegetables
  • starches
  • or fruit

Refined grains and sugar are nowhere in there.

There are basically three benefits to our carbs:

  • energy
  • fiber
  • micronutrients

The current trend in strength training is to keep carbs as low as you can. Some even go as far to say, “There is no specific need for carbs, only fat and protein.” This is true. If you were locked up in a prison camp, you would not die on a diet of only protein and fat. But you would also not thrive. The fatal flaw with low or no-carb diets is gluconeogenesis. There is no way you can sustain a very low or no-carb diet without the continuous loss of muscle.

Parts of the brain, red blood cells, the tops of the kidneys and a few other areas of the body are only capable of using carbs for fuel. So in the absence of adequate carbs in the diet, gluconeogenesis happens. Translated into plain English, your body takes proteins from your muscles and through a long process turns them into carbs. During this process, protein synthesis in the whole body drops dramatically. This happens after about 5 days without carbs.

The bottom line?

Carbs are a great source of energy, and our only source of energy for anaerobic activities like GST. Furthermore, there is no population in the world who has avoided carbs voluntarily. If we were to construct a diet based off of anthropological evidence, then I would like to bring up the Kithavis. Their diet is 69% carbs, and they are tall, lean and healthy. The Papua New Guineans and the Okinawan diet are similar: 85% of their calories come from starch. Okinawan has the highest rate of centenarians in the world, as opposed to the Inuits, who had some of the shortest lifespans when they followed their traditional no-carb diet.

Again, starches and fruit are a great energy source. Refined grains and sugar are not.

The carbs we recommend also contain fiber. There are basically two types of fiber: insoluble and soluble. We are going to throw a third type in there because of its similarities: resistant starch. Soluble sources are nuts and fruit, insoluble sources are dark green leafy vegetables, and resistant starch comes from potatoes and rice.

All three are fermented by gut flora producing short-chain fatty acids, which provides a clean energy source that later down the road aids the body in using fat for fuel. These acids are what prevent colon cancer. Soluble fiber can reduce cholesterol. Insoluble will aid in removing toxins or waste, possibly the most important role of fiber. Combined, they all improve gut function. Eat your vegetables with lunch and dinner and that will meet your fiber requirement. The claims of needing 50g daily is ridiculous.

Finally carbs -- specifically vegetables and fruit -- provide some nutrients that are just about impossible to get anywhere else. Vegetables are the pound-for-pound king of micronutrient density. Fruit isn’t far behind. These nutrients fight inflammation, slow aging, improve gut health and immune function, and help to stabilize blood sugar.

All carbs end up as glucose in the blood. Glucose is essential for energy and subsequently optimal function. Your body has a relatively small glucose storage unit; in its storage form, glucose is called glycogen. We want to use a combination of this glycogen and body fat to fuel the body’s activities. This is the toughest part of nutrition. The good new is, you have already been doing it. Just keep doing it!

description: 2-4/1-2 thumb size portions of a healthy fat with lunch
detailedDesc:
We are going to portion size fat. About two fingers is a good amount of fat to eat.

Fat is extremely hard to measure. For example, say that you are having a steak salad. You cooked the steak on the stove in a bit of coconut oil. In the salad you have gorgonzola or blue cheese crumbles, and olive oil for dressing.

The amount of fat in the cheese, the coconut oil the steak was cooked in and the olive oil dressing is pretty hard to measure. So you are going to have to do a little estimating with this step.

Two fingers is an approximate measurement in that case, but more accurate measurement is pretty easy if you are going to eat something like an avocado. A quarter to half of an avocado fits into my definition of close to two fingers. One is a little more, one is a little less.

Nuts are also a possibility, but I want you to use nuts for when you’re in a bind. Nuts are a good fat, but they’re not a great fat. The anti-nutrient phytic acid is one of the reasons we stay away from most grains, and there are also quite high amounts of this acid in nuts. But nuts do have some redeeming qualities, so don’t avoid them completely. Just use them when you need quick, convenient fat. Lunch shouldn’t be one of those times.

Fish that comes from cold water like salmon or whitefish are also great fat choices. They contain high amounts of omega-3 fatty acids. But it can be hard to bring fish to work; it doesn’t generally taste good when cold, and you get some funny looks when trying to heat it up because of the smell. If you’re eating out, fish is a good choice, but I would avoid bringing it to work.

Good luck.
lesson:
Protein is important because it contains nitrogen. The Earth has many sources of nitrogen; however, the only form a human can metabolize is from individual proteins or amino acids.

Muscle growth, connective tissue quality (aka mobility), cell replacement and tissue repair (aka recovery) all require protein. But protein is not just for athletes. If you want to have healthy-looking hair and skin, those are both protein structures. All of the structural proteins in your body turn over, meaning when damaged they repair or completely replace themselves with newer proteins. It’s important that we match the body’s protein breakdown with our protein intake. Eating protein at meals will accomplish this.

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Think of protein like a Lego house and amino acids as the individual Legos. There are 20 amino acids; like Legos, different configurations of those amino acids in different sizes and amounts are what make up proteins like steak or chicken. Nine of the amino acids are indispensable or essential, meaning they fall in the category of water and oxygen as “must haves.” The other 11 are important as well, but they can be manufactured by the essential 9 when there’s a shortage of them. This does not mean they don’t have specific, vital functions. It just means you won’t die without them.

For a protein to be considered “complete,” it must contain all 9 of the essential amino acids. Eggs, red meat, seafood, poultry and full-fat milk contain all of the essential amino acids.

If a food has some but not all 9, it’s considered an incomplete protein. These include starches, vegetables and fruit, but you aren’t eating those foods for their protein content, so it’s not much of a concern.

It is important to eat protein with each meal, because the only protein storage units in your body are your muscles. There are small amounts of amino acids floating around in the blood, but once used, the remainder of protein needed for critical functions like breathing comes from your muscles. Your body’s main goal is survival, not looking good.

That does not mean that you should cram as much protein down your mouth as you can. There’s no real point. Eating too much protein will just result in the process of gluconeogenesis, which basically converts protein to glucose.

Among complete proteins, some are better than others. There are a number of ways to measure the quality of a protein source. For example, the nitrogen or amino acid retention of a specific food is a good indication of its availability to the body, but neither of those take into account co-founding nutrients and other benefits of that food source. Take beef from grass-fed cows. The nitrogen and amino acid retention is very similar to beef from grain-fed cows, but the grass-fed has tons more vitamins, minerals and omega-3 fatty acids, making it a far better choice. When selecting animal proteins, always go for grass-fed or wild-caught sources.

Animal proteins are all optimal in essential amino acids, but they also have some nutrients that are pretty hard to find anywhere else, like vitamin B12. It plays its biggest role in your brain and is closely involved in helping DHA with the myelin process. Remember, the myelin process is the omega-3 fatty acid DHA wrapping neural circuits to make them fire faster and harder. Vitamins A (retinoids) and D are pretty much exclusively found in meat. Vitamin D is most concentrated in cold-water fish, which have a receptor site on every cell in the body. There is nothing vitamin D does not positively affect. Lastly, animal proteins contain zinc. Most concentrated in red meat, the immune system relies heavily on zinc for optimal function. Zinc is also potent in the recovery process.

Remember, eating complete protein sources at your meals is the best way to get all 9 of the essential as well as plenty of the other 11 non-essential amino acids.

When you are choosing your protein, you want sources like grass-fed beef or wild-caught salmon that are high in co-founding nutrients like vitamin D and omega-3 fatty acids. Incorporating protein into your meals allows for improved mobility, recovery, and muscle growth -- all important to maximizing your training sessions.

description: 2-3/1-2 cupped handfuls of starch with dinner
detailedDesc:
Our dinner plate is full up after this step. We are eating somewhere between 1 and 2 fistfuls of vegetables, a palm to a full hand of protein, and now starch.

Of the three things we have available for dinner, starch is the easiest to overeat, so don’t get creative with your measuring!

For the sake of keeping it simple, we are going to use our fist again. We are after the approximate size of 1 to 2 fists of starch, or carbs, with dinner. Same as vegetables. Pretty easy, right?

Another consideration is some carbs are more dense than others. One fist of rice is twice the amount of carbs as the same amount of acorn squash. It’s not necessarily a bad thing to eat two fists of rice, but like all carbs, you have to earn ‘em. If you’re training hard, no problem -- and you should be, so this is not an issue. Remember, you need those starches to fuel your training sessions and, more importantly, to recover from them.

Also, don’t get freaked out about overeating starch if you are going by the serving guidelines. We are really only eating carbs at dinner and lunch, so eating too much is almost impossible if you stick with the serving sizes.

We have our vegetables, protein and now our starches dialed in, all of them working in harmony in the name of better nutrition. This is the first complete meal with appropriate portions. Congrats on making it this far! Stick in there -- this is where it gets fun!
lesson:
We are currently sleeping 7 hours a night or more. Now, for the the second sleep goal, I want you to bump that up.

Your new goal is to get a minimum of 8 hours of sleep every night.

Training is added stress on the body, above and beyond the normal work day. To progress in training, we need to recover from training. Optimal recovery times for athletes is 8 hours minimum.

As we talked about before, sleep is when the house cleaners, construction workers and maintenance men come out. The more stress we induce, the more time they need to do their job. Pretty straightforward.

Sleep is your biggest recovery tool.

When your training consists of complex skills like GST, the whole neuromuscular unit is trained and requires recovery. These are the specific muscles that are working, the brain controlling them and the nervous system that connects them. In many cases, the muscles themselves recover faster than the nervous system. Your muscles recover with glycogen and other nutrients, but your brain and nervous system best recover with sleep.

Sleep’s effects on recovery reaches further than just the nervous system. Testosterone and growth hormone are equally reliant on sleep for renewal. Male or female, increased levels of those two = progress in the gym + improved fat loss.

Without exception, sleep is your biggest recovery tool. Focus on making those 8 hours of sleep the best you can. No light, no electronics, just sleep. Eight hours.

Good luck.

description: 2/1 palm size portions of animal protein with lunch
detailedDesc:
Two more steps after this one!

Lunch protein portion: Do I need to remind you of the importance of protein? The nine essential amino acids that we can’t manufacture in our body, we have to get from food. Those essential nutrients are pretty much only found in meat -- B12, vitamin D and so on. Protein at even intervals throughout the day is a must -- breakfast, lunch and dinner.

Your lunch portion should be the same as dinner; a palm or a hand of protein.
lesson:
Today is Prep Day!

One time a week I want you to make dinner big enough to have leftovers for lunch. For dinner you are eating a protein, starch, vegetable. For lunch you are eating a protein, starch, vegetable and fat. Basically we want to make enough protein and starch at dinner to have some left over for lunch tomorrow. While dinner is cooking you can put your salad together and add in your fat.

The reason I want you to do this is because in the near future I want you to have the ability to control 100% of the food you eat and develop confidence in the kitchen. Often times when you eat chicken, rice and broccoli in a restaurant the chicken is feed lot chicken with poor nutrient levels, the rice often times is cooked in industrial vegetable oil(not a good thing). The idea with this step is to put the control in your hands and like every other Thrive step this is one at a time. I want you to pack lunch 1 time a week for now.

Some things to think about:

  1. Cook foods that will taste good for lunch. Choose foods that travel well, if you don’t have a means to heat your food up at work then choose something that is good cold. If you work in a corporate setting in America, throwing some smelly fish in the microwave may not be the best option.
  2. Don’t make foods that require more time to eat than you have. Choose foods that can be enjoyable eating with the time you have for lunch. If you work at home this will be different than if you eat on the subway. A steak requires that you warm it up, cut with a knife and have a decent amount of time to eat it. Really easy to eat items are ground beef and rice.
  3. Pack lunch night before so easy to grab and go. Get a designated ‘lunch box’. When you are cooking dinner pack up your lunch and everything you need so in the morning you can grab and go. Time in the morning is always limited and you still have to eat breakfast so take the time and front load this work. Put your meal, salad, utensils and snack(if you eat one) in the lunch box. In the morning drop in the ice pack if applicable and go!
  4. Develop your go to meals, start with one then add start creating your list of go-tos to put into rotation. In all reality there is only about 6-10 go to meals a person has. There is nothing wrong with in the beginning - eating the same meal every Wednesday night because its a good lunch for tomorrow. With time and repetition you will develop more go-to meals and off shoots of those go to meals. Keep it simple.

Let’s get started!

These are 2 good bang for your buck meals that take into account cost, prep, cook time, effort and clean up. I recommend you start with one of these so you don’t stress yourself out by biting off more than you can chew(pun intended) your first time.

  1. All oven option: 1/4 chicken with the skin on, potato. Set the oven to 400. While it’s pre-heating put enough chicken quarters (leg and thigh) for dinner and lunch onto a glass baking dish. Brush lightly with butter then season liberally with salt and pepper. Easiest is baked potato, wash potatoes, poke with fork and place on baking sheet. Make sure the chicken is skin side up. Put the chicken on one rack and the potatoes on another. Both will cook for 50min. Chicken should come out with nice crispy skin and the potatoes soft but not mushy.
  2. BBQ Salmon, asparagus and rice: Pre-heat grill to high medium heat. Start some white rice, go basic or try to use 1/2 chicken stock - 1/2 water and a bay leaf when you cook it. Get the rice on the stove, takes 17min. After that brush the salmon with a light coat of olive oil(top only) then season with salt, pepper. Brush the asparagus and salt it as well(its okay the olive oil won’t burn in the 6 min we cook this). Generally salmon takes about 10 min to cook. You will start to see the color turn pink on the edge and work its way in. Take it off the grill before its 100% cooked or your salmon will be dry. When the salmon is about half done put on the asparagus on the grill. When you take them both off cover and let sit for a min. Dish up rice, asparagus and salmon and eat. After your done with this dinner is a good time to package up lunch. Don’t forget the salad.

Okay guys, give it a shot and let me know how it goes in the forum. Feel free to post pictures and ask questions, also take a look at what others are doing.

detailedDesc:
This is the last addition of portions to our meals. By now you have squared up all your meals into proper ratios of vegetables, fats, starches and protein.

In this course, we have not taken anything away. We have focused on building the foundations of nutrition. I’m hoping by now we have squeezed all the sub-optimal foods out of your diet. What we don’t get rid of here, we will get rid of in Level Two.

Lunch comes at the halfway point of most people’s work day. You still have to go out there and play another half. For that you will need your brain and muscles. We have already maxed out our lower carb stretch of the day from dinner last night to now. We need to get some starches to feed the brain if we want it to keep working. Starches are our energy. Let’s make sure we are getting enough.
lesson:
The best thing you can do for yourself pre- and post-workout is to follow your nutritional and lifestyle steps:

  • Quality meals,
  • good sleep,
  • hydration,
  • and the absence of junk food.

The basics are the basics because they’re the non-negotiable things you have to get right to be successful. Right now, I really want you to focus on mastering these steps. We will cover supplements in detail in Level Two. Don’t worry, you will get there. We just need to do things in order.

At this level, supplements are a distraction. You are making big changes in lifestyle and nutrition habits. That is where you need to focus 100% of your energy. A pyramid can only be as high is the base is wide. We need to focus on the foundation before moving on.

Supplements do play a role in performance, but not here in Level One. Here it’s a distraction more than anything. So what does your workout supplement protocol look like right now? It’s filling your plate with as many nutrient-dense foods as possible, following each of the steps as they are presented, and ensuring you’re filling in the lifestyle pieces by meeting your sleep and hydration goals.

There is no supplement that can match a healthy lifestyle and good nutrition.

If you feel like you need a workout supplement because you are low on energy, it is time to take a step back and evaluate your consistency with the nutrition steps. Take it back to the basics. How’s your daily water intake? Look at your sleep quality. What about your meals at this stage in the process? If you feel like you “need” more, it’s probably because you’re missing a step or getting lax somewhere along the way.

Alright, guys, keep up the good work. We are almost done.

detailedDesc:
This is an open-ended goal, not a step. It is also the last part of Level One.

We have portioned out lunch and dinner.

For breakfast I only want your portion goal to be: Eat a big enough breakfast to make it to lunch. For me this is 6 eggs, or salmon and yogurt. I also want you to make healthy fats and protein as much of your breakfast as you can. In Level Two, I am going to take away morning carbs all together.

This is an open-ended goal because for some of you this will be dramatic lifestyle change. For others, you may already be doing this step.

How hungry you get between breakfast and lunch is a function of how good of a fat burner you are.

  • Efficient = No problem. You will access your fat stores.
  • Carb-aholic = You will have a lot of problems. You lack the metabolic machinery to burn glucose and body fat. This step is going to be hard for you.

You have two choices: DO IT OR QUIT.

We are effectively turning you into 1/2 diesel engine and 1/2 petrol engine.

Being a little bit hungry during the day is okay! I eat at 6:30am. By 10:30, I’m hungry; lunch is at 11. Being hungry encourages your body to look within for energy. If you are a good fat burner, that is what your body will use. If you insist on staying a carb-aholic, then yeah, you’re a slave to your diet.

Last step: Congrats - solid nutrition.

No free lunch, just hard work and consistency.

You should have a sense of pride and accomplishment for the hard work you have put in to complete this course, and your commitment to personal excellence is now stronger than it was when you started. We know that some of the habits you've now formed will be truly life-changing.

Be happy with where you are now. You are actually walking the walk. Nutritionally, this is a great place to be for the rest of your life.

Good work, guys!
